newsitem.title: UK: Grobbelaar says wanted to reveal bribes sting.
newsitem.headline: Grobbelaar says wanted to reveal bribes sting.

text.p: Former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar said on Friday he had pretended to agree to rig soccer matches so he could get details of what was on offer and then report the approach to the authorities.

Grobbelaar also told a court in the city of Winchester that during the 14 years he spent with Liverpool it was common knowledge that players bet on matches they were involved in. This practice is illegal under Football Association rules.

The case against Grobbelaar is based on secretly taped conversations in which he appeared to agree to a suggestion from former business partner Chris Vincent that he rig matches for a mythical betting syndicate.
"I wanted to know who Vincent was working with. I went along with the charade, put in stories to make it more feasible, to find out who Vincent was talking to and tell the authorities," he said.
"Had you told anybody else what you'd done?" asked prosecutor David Calvert Smith.

"No," replied Grobbelaar, who is also accused along with former Wimbledon keeper Hans Segers, ex-Wimbledon and Aston Villa striker John Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim of rigging games to benefit an Asian betting syndicate.
All four deny the charges, although both keepers say they were paid in cash by Lim for providing match forecasts.
Grobbelaar was filmed picking up a pack of money which Vincent had given to him on behalf of the syndicate. He told the court he intended to hand it in to the authorities.
"Why was it that you declined to meet the people involved?" Calvert Smith asked.
"Because they would have known who I was," the keeper said.
Grobbelaar said by the time he started working with Lim, he had already forecast games for a Norwegian newspaper and a South African radio station.
"Are you saying that receiving cash from Lim in various hotels and airport lounges is the equivalent of having a column in a newspaper or appearing on the radio?" asked Calvert Smith.
"Not exactly the same," Grobbelaar conceded. But he said betting on games was common among professional players.
"Some players went to the bookmakers, sometimes on the day of the game, while some gave money to friends to do it for them," he said.
"It was fairly common practice. They would put money on the first goalscorer and maybe to get a 3-1 win," he said.
"Did you know players weren't supposed to bet?" asked Calvert Smith. "No," said Grobbelaar.
"I suggest that a man of your experience and intelligence must have known," retorted the prosecutor.

Earlier in the day the court watched a recording of a 3-3 draw which Liverpool played out with Manchester United in early January 1994. On the covert tapes Grobbelaar appeared to admit he had tried to lose the game.
Asked by lawyer Rodney Klevan whether he had tried to throw this game or any other, Grobbelaar replied: "I didn't do anything improper in any of the games."

Segers' lawyer Desmond De Silva then asked Grobbelaar to comment on the last goal of a game between Everton and Wimbledon in May 1994 which gave Everton a 3-2 win and preserved their place in the premier division.
The ball seemed to slip between Segers' arms and trickle into the net, but Grobbelaar said the ball had changed direction after hitting another player as well as a divot.
"Could another goalkeeper have saved it?" De Silva asked. "I don't think so, no," Grobbelaar replied.
